Two or more breaches between the same two events (e.g. two strokes) count as one penalty – the higher one if they differ.

Your marker certifies your hole scores; you check them, sign and hand in the scorecard promptly. You are not responsible for adding up or for the handicap calculation done by the committee – but your handicap on the card must be right.
You may not add clubs during the round to replace ones you started with, and you must not borrow a club from anyone playing on the course.
A club you damage in anger may not be replaced, but you may keep using it as damaged.
If your ball falls off the tee before a stroke or you knock it off at address, re-tee it without penalty.
You may change balls between holes. During a hole you may substitute a ball only when taking relief or when a Rule allows it (e.g. a cut or cracked ball).
If you damage the course while searching (e.g. trampling grass), there is no penalty as long as it is part of a fair search; you must not improve conditions on purpose.
If you improve conditions in breach of the Rule you may restore them before the stroke and avoid the penalty – unless you bent or broke a growing thing, or moved a boundary object.
No penalty when you accidentally move your ball: while searching for it, on the putting green, while applying a Rule (e.g. marking), or because of an accident not caused by you.
Your caddie may stand behind you on your line before your stance, but must move away once you begin taking your stance – also on the putting green.
You may not have someone shade you from the sun or shelter you from rain while making the stroke – you may do it yourself.
If a ball played from outside the green comes to rest on a person or animal, drop it where it would have come to rest (on the green: place it).
Allowed in a bunker: lean on a club, place clubs or equipment in the bunker, smooth sand to care for the course (not to improve the stroke), dig in with your feet for a stance.
If your ball or ball-marker on the green is accidentally moved by anyone, replace it without penalty.
Wrong green: when your ball lies on a green other than the one of the hole played, or it interferes with your stance, you must take free relief off it.
Attended flagstick: deliberately letting your ball hit the person attending it or the flagstick held by them costs the general penalty; by accident there is no penalty.
A ball resting against the flagstick in the hole is holed if any part of it is below the surface of the green.

The original lie is altered (e.g. sand pressed): in a bunker re-create it as closely as possible; elsewhere place the ball on the nearest spot with the most similar lie within one club-length, not nearer the hole.
If the dropped ball touches a person or equipment before it hits the ground, drop again without penalty. If it hits someone after landing and still stops in the relief area, play it as it lies.
The relief area is measured with your longest club except the putter, from the reference point the Rule gives (nearest point of complete relief, the point where the ball crossed the edge …).
Movable obstructions in a penalty area or bunker may also be removed; if the ball moves, replace it without penalty.

Interference: the condition touches or holds your ball, physically interferes with your stance or area of swing, or – on the green only – is on your line of play. Mere interference with your line of play elsewhere gives no relief.

No relief when it is clearly unreasonable to play the ball (e.g. your ball is in a bush and a sprinkler head is under your foot) or when interference only exists because of an unusual stance or swing.
Ball not found but known or virtually certain to be in an abnormal course condition: take relief from the point where it last crossed the edge of the condition.
No relief when the ball is embedded in sand in a part of the general area not cut to fairway height or less, or when playing it is clearly unreasonable.
A ball is in a penalty area when any part of it touches the ground or anything inside the edge, or is above it. The edge extends up and down.
Playing it as it lies: you may ground your club, touch the water or ground and take practice swings – the same as in the general area.
Ball not found but known or virtually certain to be in the penalty area: take relief from the point where it last crossed the edge. Not virtually certain: it is a lost ball (Rule 18.2).
A ball is out of bounds only when all of it lies outside the boundary edge. The inside edge of the white stakes or line marks the boundary.
Announce it clearly (“provisional ball”). Playing another ball without saying so makes it the ball in play under stroke and distance.
You may keep playing the provisional ball until you reach the area where the original is likely to be; once it is played from a point nearer the hole than that area, it becomes the ball in play.
Back-on-the-line: pick a reference point on the line from the hole through the ball (any distance back); drop within one club-length of it, not nearer the hole.

In stroke play announce that you play two balls and which one you want to count if the Rules allow it, and report the facts to the committee before returning your scorecard – otherwise disqualification.
A ball that breaks into pieces from a stroke: the stroke does not count – play another ball without penalty from where that stroke was made.

Allowed: weather information, the Rules, your own notes and data from earlier rounds, gloves, a towel. Not allowed in a competition: a device that recommends a club or a line of play – like the caddie in this app. Distances are fine.
The committee may set a pace of play policy with time limits. A group that has lost its place should close the gap or let the group behind play through.
Signals: one long tone means stop immediately; three short tones mean a normal suspension – you may finish the hole you are playing; two short tones mean play resumes.
When play resumes, continue from where you stopped; if you lifted the ball, replace it (or another ball) on the marked spot.
A tee must not be longer than 101.6 mm. Do not move the tee-markers to improve your stance or swing (general penalty).
A ball in play that is still in the teeing area after a stroke (e.g. a topped shot) may be lifted and teed up again without penalty.

Match play: on the first tee the draw decides the honour, later the winner of the last hole has it (a halved hole keeps the honour). Stroke play: the lowest score on the last hole (net score in a net competition).
A provisional ball or another ball from the tee is played after everyone else has played their first stroke.
A ball may not be assumed to be yours just because of where it lies. If you cannot identify it, it is lost – so put your own mark on your ball before the round.
You may lift the ball only if you reasonably believe it could be yours; you no longer need to tell anyone beforehand.
Do not make a stroke with your feet deliberately on either side of, or touching, the line of play or its extension behind the ball.
Do not hit a moving ball – except a ball falling off the tee, one moving in water in a penalty area, or one that starts moving after the backswing began.
Your caddie may mark and lift your ball on the green without asking you; elsewhere only with your permission. Your caddie may not decide that the ball is unplayable or take relief (drop) for you.
A ball on soil or grass inside the bunker without touching sand is not in the bunker; a wall or face of grass or soil is not part of it.
Lifting without marking, marking wrongly or playing with the ball-marker still in place: one penalty stroke.
When correcting the mistake you may also change to another relief option or another Rule.
A serious breach means a significant advantage, e.g. a much shorter shot. To correct it, finish the hole with a ball played from the right place; the strokes and penalties with the wrong ball count.
Loose impediments are natural objects that are not fixed: stones, leaves, twigs, insects, worms, dung, casts. Sand and loose soil count only on the green; dew, frost and water never.
You may do this at any time, for any reason – e.g. after a bad shot. The original ball is then no longer in play.
You do not have to find the ball to declare it unplayable – but without the ball only stroke and distance is left.
If you pick up or do not hole out, you score zero points on that hole – no disqualification.
If you do not hole out, you get the maximum score for that hole.
If the wrong partner plays: general penalty; correct it with the right partner from where the wrong stroke was made (in stroke play before the next tee, otherwise disqualification).

In the inbox: the tray top right, beside the sun mode. A green number says how many wait. In it: a request to join your round ("Let in" right there), a card someone asks to correct (as the host you confirm it right there), a friend request, invitations to a round, a game or bets, a new bet against you, a payment to you ("Received"), your scorecard to sign, a 5+5+10 challenge, rounds to check & sign and results to confirm – a tap goes straight there.
How do I change the language?

In your profile, "Language": English, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Finnish, Polish, Japanese or Chinese. At the first start the app takes your phone's language when it is one of them – otherwise English.

Ball flight & misses
Why the ball slices, hooks, pushes, pulls, tops or shanks – and the cure.

The ball tells you what the club did. Two numbers explain every curve: where the club face points at impact (that sets the start direction – about 75–85 % of it) and how the face sits relative to the swing path (that sets the curve). A face open to the path curves the ball right (fade, slice), a face closed to the path curves it left (draw, hook). If you understand this, you can read every shot and fix it yourself.
New ball flight laws (TrackMan): the start direction comes mostly from the face, the curve from the difference between face and path.
About 4 of 5 amateurs slice: face open to an out-to-in path.
Hitting the toe makes the ball curve left (gear effect, woods), hitting the heel makes it curve right.
A shank comes from the hosel – the club is closer to the ball at impact than at address, not further away.
The nine ball flights
Starts straight: straight, fade (soft curve right), draw (soft curve left).
Starts right: push (stays right), push-slice (curves further right), push-draw (comes back).
Starts left: pull (stays left), pull-hook (curves further left), pull-fade (comes back).
A fade or a draw are good shots – a slice and a hook curve too much.
The slice

The ball starts left or straight and curves strongly right. Cause: a face that is open to the path, usually with a path from out to in. Typical reasons: a weak grip, shoulders open at address, the downswing started with the shoulders (“over the top”), no release of the forearms. First fix the grip and the alignment; then work on the path from the inside.
Slice: starts slightly left, curves strongly right.
The hook

The ball curves strongly left. Cause: a face closed to the path, often a strong grip or the hands flipping over through impact, or a path too much from the inside. Fixes: check the grip (fewer knuckles), let the body keep turning through the ball, hold the finish with the face pointing to the sky.
Hook: starts slightly right, curves strongly left.

Shank: weight moves to the toes, hands move away from the body → weight on the heels, tee or headcover outside the ball.
Sky ball with woods: too steep → ball forward, wider swing.

Basics: grip, stance, alignment
The set-up decides before the swing starts – and you can check it alone.

Most swing faults start before the swing: a grip that opens the face, aiming right without noticing, the ball in the wrong place. The good news: the set-up is static – you can check it in a mirror, with alignment sticks or a photo, and it costs no talent. Teachers say that a large part of all faults they see come from grip, alignment and ball position.
An error of 2° in the aim of the face moves a 150 m shot about 5 m off line.
Most amateurs aim right of the target (right-handers) and then pull the ball back with an out-to-in swing – the start of the slice.
Grip pressure: about 4–5 on a scale of 10 for full swings – firm enough to control the club, loose enough for speed.
The grip
Lead hand (left for right-handers): the club lies across the fingers, from the base of the little finger to the middle of the index finger – not in the palm.
Looking down you see 2–3 knuckles of the lead hand; the V between thumb and index finger points to the trail shoulder.
Trail hand: the lifeline covers the lead thumb; its V also points to the trail shoulder.
Overlap (little finger on the lead index finger), interlock (little finger hooked) or ten-finger grip – all are fine; choose what feels secure.
“Weak” grip (fewer knuckles visible) tends to open the face → slice; “strong” grip closes it → hook.

Bend forward from the hips (not the waist), back straight, bottom out.
Knees slightly flexed, weight on the middle of the feet.
Arms hang freely from the shoulders; a hand width between the handle and the thighs.
Stance about shoulder width for a 7-iron, wider for the driver, narrower for wedges.

Pick an intermediate target – a leaf or a divot 1 m in front of the ball on the line – and align to that; it is much easier than to a flag 150 m away.

Bunker
Greenside, fairway bunker and the fried egg – you hit the sand, not the ball.

The greenside bunker shot is the only shot in golf where you do not hit the ball: the club enters the sand a few centimetres behind it and throws a cushion of sand – with the ball on it – onto the green. With the right set-up and a full, confident swing it is easier than most chips. The fairway bunker is the opposite: here the ball must be hit first, cleanly.
Tour players get out and save par from greenside bunkers about 50 % of the time (sand saves); a handicap 20 player about 10–15 %, and often needs two shots to get out.
The club enters the sand about 3–5 cm (two fingers) behind the ball and leaves it about 10 cm in front of it.
The bounce – the angle of the sole of the sand wedge – stops the club from digging in. Opening the face uses more bounce.
Rule: you may not touch the sand with the club before the stroke (no grounding, no practice swing in the sand) – a two-stroke penalty in stroke play.
Set-up in the greenside bunker
Open the face of the sand wedge first, then take your grip.
Stance wider than for a pitch, slightly open; dig your feet in a little for a firm stand (and to feel the sand).
Ball forward of centre (towards the lead heel).
Weight slightly on the lead side, knees flexed, a little lower than normal.
Look at a spot in the sand two fingers behind the ball – not at the ball.
sand
body line open
The club enters behind the ball and exits in front of it – a “dollar bill” of sand.
The swing

Swing along your (open) body line with a long, relaxed swing – about the length of a 40–50 m pitch for a 10 m bunker shot. The club enters the sand at the spot behind the ball and splashes through to a full finish. The face stays open: in the finish it points to the sky. Never slow down – the sand brakes the club enough. Arm speed, not a flick of the hands, gives a consistent result.
The length is controlled by the length of the swing and how much sand you take – not by hitting softer.

Chipping
Low shots around the green: landing spot, club choice, clean contact.

A chip flies a short distance and then rolls to the hole – like a long putt with loft. It is the shot that saves pars: a player with handicap 20 misses about 13–15 greens per round and needs a chip almost every time. Three things decide: the landing spot (where the ball should touch down), the club (how far it rolls after landing) and clean contact (ball first, then a light brush of the grass).
Rule of thumb for carry : roll on a flat green – SW 1:1, PW 1:2, 9-iron 1:3, 8-iron 1:4, 7-iron 1:5. Uphill less roll, downhill more.
“As low as possible, as high as necessary”: a rolling ball is easier to control than a flying one – putt if you can, chip if you cannot putt, pitch only if you must.
Tour players get up and down around 60 % of the time; a player with handicap 20 only about 15–20 %.
From 10 m off the green the average amateur leaves the chip about 2.5–3 m from the hole – getting it within 1 m saves about one stroke per round.
The set-up
Narrow stance (feet a hand width apart), slightly open to the target.
Ball in the middle or slightly back (towards the trail foot).
About 60–70 % of the weight on the lead foot – and it stays there.
Hands slightly ahead of the ball, grip down the club a little.
Stand closer to the ball, the club a bit more upright – like a putt.
short flight
The stroke

A chip is a putting stroke with a lofted club: the shoulders rock, the arms and the club move together, the wrists stay quiet. The club head brushes the grass under the ball – no scooping, no lifting. The lead wrist stays flat through impact, the handle leads. Back and through are about the same length, and the club accelerates gently.
The loft of the club lifts the ball – you never have to help it up.
Landing spot and club choice

Look at the chip like a putt: where must the ball land so that it rolls the rest? Usually a spot about 1 m onto the green, where the surface is even. Then choose the club whose carry : roll fits the ratio of carry to roll. One technique – several clubs: the motion stays the same, only the club changes. Many good players chip with SW, PW, 9 and 7-iron; beginners do well with one or two clubs.

Special chips
From the fringe: putt it (the Texas wedge) or use a hybrid or fairway wood like a putter.
From the rough: steeper stroke, ball a little back, more loft – the grass slows the club and the ball comes out with less spin and rolls more.
Ball against the collar of the rough: hit it with the leading edge of a wedge at the ball’s equator (“bellied wedge”) or with a putter.
Uphill to the hole: land the ball further and use less loft; downhill: more loft and land it short.
Practise like this
Always with a landing target – a ring, a towel or a tee – never just at the hole.
Change club, lie and target after every few balls (random practice is closer to the course).
Finish with a game where you putt out – the up-and-down is what counts.
